entry: Highly toxic, flammable [[Chemical compound|chemical compound]] with the formula HCN, also called prussic acid. It boils at 25.6 °C (78.1 °F), slightly above room temperature, and is produced on an industrial scale as a precursor to [[Polymer|polymers]] and pharmaceuticals. Large-scale applications include the production of [[Potassium cyanide]], used in mining, and adiponitrile, used in [[Plastic|plastics]]. It is more toxic than solid cyanide compounds because of its volatile nature. French chemist Pierre Macquer first isolated it in 1752 from [[Prussian blue]].

Inorganic compound with the formula HF, a colorless gas or liquid that dissolves in water to form [[Hydrofluoric acid|hydrofluoric acid]]. It is the principal industrial source of [[Fluorine|fluorine]] and an important feedstock for pharmaceuticals and [[Polymer|polymers]] such as [[Polytetrafluoroethylene|polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE)]]. Strong hydrogen bonding makes it boil near room temperature, far above other hydrogen halides. It is extremely dangerous: it readily forms highly corrosive hydrofluoric acid on contact with moisture and can cause blindness by rapid destruction of the corneas.

Chemical compound with the formula H₂O₂, the simplest peroxide. In pure form it is a very pale blue, viscous liquid, though dilute solutions appear colorless. For consumer use it is sold as a 3%–6% by weight solution in water, and it serves as an oxidizer, bleaching agent and antiseptic. Concentrated solutions decompose explosively when heated, and the compound has been used as a monopropellant and oxidizer in [[Rocket|rocketry]]. Its extrapolated boiling point is 150.2 °C (302.4 °F), and heating to that temperature can cause potentially explosive decomposition. It breaks down into water and oxygen when exposed to light and rapidly in the presence of organic or reactive compounds. It occurs in biological systems, including the human body, and enzymes that use or decompose it are classified as peroxidases.

Colorless, toxic and flammable gas with the formula H₂S. Trace amounts in air have a foul odor of rotten eggs. It is toxic because it inhibits [[Cellular respiration|cellular respiration]], a mechanism similar to that of [[Hydrogen cyanide|hydrogen cyanide]], and high exposures can cause death. It is often produced by microbes breaking down organic matter without oxygen, as in [[Swamp|swamps]] and sewers, and also occurs in volcanic gases and natural gas deposits. It is slightly denser than air, acts as a weak acid in water, and can form explosive mixtures with air.

Branch of applied sciences concerned with measuring and describing the physical features of [[Ocean|oceans]], [[Sea|seas]], coastal areas, [[Lake|lakes]] and [[River|rivers]], and predicting how they change over time. Its primary purpose is navigational safety, though it also supports economic development, security, scientific research and environmental protection. Surveys record tides, currents, waves and seabed hazards such as rocks, shoals and reefs. The field began with charts made by individual mariners, often closely held secrets. As transoceanic trade grew, governments and navies commissioned surveys and founded dedicated hydrographic offices. In the [[United Kingdom]], the Admiralty appointed Alexander Dalrymple as Hydrographer in 1795, and its first chart, of Quiberon Bay in [[Brittany]], appeared in 1800.

Scientific study of the movement, distribution and management of water on [[Earth]] and other planets. A practitioner is called a hydrologist and draws on earth science, civil or environmental engineering, and physical geography. Hydrology subdivides into surface water hydrology, groundwater hydrology (hydrogeology) and marine hydrology. Applications include calculating rainfall and runoff, predicting [[Flood|floods]] and [[Drought|droughts]], designing [[Dam|dams]] and [[Bridge|bridges]], planning irrigation, and providing drinking water. Ancient Egyptians invented basin irrigation, Mesopotamian towns built high earthen walls against flooding, and the Greeks and Romans built aqueducts. Hydrological research informs environmental engineering, policy and planning.

Combined body of water found on, under and above the surface of a planet, minor planet or natural satellite. [[Earth|Earth's]] hydrosphere has existed for about 4 billion years and continues to change as seafloor spreading and continental drift rearrange land and ocean. It has been estimated at 1.386 billion cubic kilometers (333 million cubic miles) of water, including water in the atmosphere, in [[Glacier|glaciers]], lakes and rivers, and in living organisms. Saltwater accounts for 97.5% of this total. Of the fresh water, 68.9% is ice and permanent snow cover, 30.8% is groundwater, and only 0.3% is in easily accessible lakes, reservoirs and river systems. Oceans cover about 71% of Earth's surface. Water moves between reservoirs through the [[Water cycle|water cycle]], driven by solar energy and gravity.

State of balance in a fluid or plastic solid at rest, in which external forces such as [[Gravity|gravity]] are offset by a pressure-gradient force. On Earth it keeps the atmosphere from collapsing into a thin, dense shell, while gravity keeps it from diffusing into [[Outer space|outer space]]. It is the criterion that distinguishes [[Dwarf planet|dwarf planets]] from small solar system bodies, and in general it causes objects in space to be spherical. In addition to the Sun, about a dozen equilibrium objects are confirmed in the [[Solar System]].

Fissure on the seabed from which geothermally heated water discharges. Vents occur near volcanically active areas, at [[Mid-ocean ridge|mid-ocean ridges]] and at hotspots. Water emerges at temperatures from 60 °C (140 °F) up to 464 °C (867 °F), against ambient water near 2 °C (36 °F). Vent areas are more biologically productive than most of the deep sea, with [[Archaea|archaea]] and chemosynthetic bacteria forming the base of a food chain that supports giant tube worms, clams, limpets and shrimp. Vents have been hypothesized to be significant in starting [[Abiogenesis|abiogenesis]]. Active vents are thought to exist on Jupiter's moon [[Europa (moon)|Europa]] and Saturn's moon [[Enceladus]].

First-generation antihistamine of the piperazine family, sold as Atarax and Vistaril among other brands. It is used for itchiness, anxiety, insomnia and nausea, including motion sickness, and works by blocking the effects of histamine. Common side effects include sleepiness, headache and dry mouth; QT prolongation is a possible serious side effect. Doses for sleep range from 25 to 100 mg, but tolerance to its [[Central nervous system|central nervous system]] effects can develop within a few days. A systematic review found that it outperforms [[Placebo|placebo]] for generalized anxiety disorder. Union Chimique Belge first made it in 1956.

Feliform [[Carnivora|carnivoran]] mammal of the family Hyaenidae, with just four living species. Despite their low diversity, hyenas are vital components of most [[Africa|African]] ecosystems. Although closer in ancestry to felines and viverrids, they resemble canids through convergent evolution: both are cursorial hunters that catch prey with their teeth rather than claws. Hyenas originated in [[Miocene|Miocene]] Eurasia 22 million years ago. Most dog-like hyena lineages declined with climate change and the arrival of canids, while bone-crushing hyenas, including the spotted, brown and striped hyenas, became top scavengers in Eurasia and Africa. Folklore often portrays them as frightening, and in some cultures their body parts are used in [[Traditional medicine|traditional medicine]].

Wide-ranging family of [[Frog|frogs]] commonly called tree frogs and their allies. Most hylids show arboreal adaptations, such as forward-facing eyes and adhesive pads on the fingers and toes, though many species are terrestrial or semiaquatic. The earliest fossils come from the [[Cretaceous]] of India and [[Wyoming]]. Hylids lay eggs in ponds, tree-hole puddles, bromeliads or on leaves over water, so that [[Tadpole|tadpoles]] drop in when they hatch. Some South American species brood eggs on the female's back. Most hylids feed on insects, and some larger species eat small vertebrates. The European tree frog (*Hyla arborea*) is common in the middle and south of Europe.

Thin mucosal membrane that surrounds or partially covers the vaginal opening. It forms part of the vulva and is similar in structure to the [[Vagina|vagina]]. Many mammals have hymens. During [[Puberty|puberty]], [[Estrogen|estrogen]] makes it very elastic, and its normal shapes range from thin and stretchy to thick and somewhat rigid; very rarely it is absent. It can tear during penetrative intercourse, usually causing pain and sometimes mild bleeding. Its state is therefore not a reliable indicator of [[Virginity|virginity]], though "virginity testing" persists in some cultures, and international health organizations condemn it as harmful.

Large order of insects comprising sawflies, [[Wasp|wasps]], [[Bee|bees]] and [[Ant|ants]]. Over 150,000 living species have been described, in addition to over 2,000 extinct ones, and many are parasitic. Females typically have an ovipositor for inserting [[Egg|eggs]] into hosts or inaccessible places, often modified into a stinger. Hymenopterans have chewing mouthparts, and most usually have two pairs of wings coupled by hooked bristles called hamuli. Their young develop through [[Metamorphosis|complete metamorphosis]], with a wormlike larval stage and an inactive pupal stage. The order originated in the Triassic, and social species appeared during the [[Cretaceous]]. The name comes from [[Ancient Greek]] words meaning membrane and wing.

Religious song written for adoration or prayer, typically addressed to a [[Deity|deity]] or deities. The word derives from Greek *hymnos*, meaning "a song of praise." Hymns also form part of other world religions, especially in the Indian subcontinent. Some of the oldest surviving examples of [[Musical notation|notated music]] are hymns with Greek texts. Ancient examples include the Sumerian Kesh temple hymn, the Egyptian Great Hymn to the Aten by Pharaoh [[Akhenaten]], and the Rigveda. Christian hymns, originally modeled on the Book of Psalms, praise God and often refer to [[Jesus]]. Many have seasonal themes for holy days such as [[Christmas]] and [[Easter]].

Alexandrian Neoplatonist philosopher, astronomer and mathematician. She was the daughter of the mathematician Theon of Alexandria and is the first female mathematician whose life is reasonably well recorded. She wrote a commentary on [[Diophantus]]'s thirteen-volume *Arithmetica*, which may survive in part, and taught philosophy and astronomy to students in [[Alexandria]], including the future bishop Synesius. Late in life she advised Orestes, the Roman prefect of Alexandria, who was in a feud with [[Cyril of Alexandria|Cyril]], the bishop of Alexandria. Rumors that she was blocking their reconciliation led a mob of Christians, under a lector named Peter, to murder her. Her death made her a "martyr for philosophy," and in the twentieth century she became an icon for [[Women's rights|women's rights]].

Smooth plane curve and one of three kinds of [[Conic section|conic section]], with two branches that are mirror images of each other. It forms when a plane cuts both halves of a double cone without passing through the apex. It is also the locus of points whose distances to two fixed foci differ by a constant. Its arms approach two asymptotes that meet at the center of symmetry. Hyperbolas describe the path of a sundial gnomon's shadow, the open orbit of an object exceeding [[Escape velocity|escape velocity]], and the scattering path of a subatomic particle. The term is believed to have been coined by [[Apollonius of Perga]], who analyzed the curve in his work on conic sections.

Analogues of the trigonometric functions, defined using the [[Hyperbola|hyperbola]] rather than the circle. The basic functions are hyperbolic sine (sinh) and hyperbolic cosine (cosh), from which tangent, cotangent, secant and cosecant are derived. Just as (cos t, sin t) traces a circle, (cosh t, sinh t) traces the right half of the unit hyperbola. The derivatives of sinh and cosh are cosh and sinh. They express Lorentz boosts as hyperbolic rotations in [[Special relativity|special relativity]] and occur in solutions of many linear differential equations, such as the one defining a catenary. Vincenzo Riccati introduced them formally in 1757, and Johann Heinrich Lambert systematized their use during the 1760s.

Practice of marrying or partnering with a spouse of higher social status, colloquially called marrying up. Originally it referred to higher socioeconomic class; today it more often means partnering with someone of higher composite mate value, especially in [[Evolutionary psychology|evolutionary psychology]]. Its antonym is hypogamy. Hindu law books refer to the concepts as anuloma and pratiloma. Early church writers sought to limit the large age gaps that hypergamous marriages could produce. Demographic research shows that educational hypergamy declined as female educational attainment surpassed men's in many developed nations.

Genus of [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]] in the family Hypericaceae, known as St. John's worts. It has a nearly worldwide distribution, missing only from tropical lowlands, deserts and polar regions. Many species are regarded as [[Invasive species|invasive]] and noxious weeds. Norman Robson, working at the [[Natural History Museum, London|Natural History Museum]] in London, produced a worldwide monograph recognizing 36 sections within the genus. Dark glands contain hypericin or pseudohypericin and give a red stain when crushed, while pale glands secrete oils. Paracelsus named the red secretions "Johannes-blut" in the 16th century, linking the plant to St. John. *Hypericum perforatum* is widely used in herbal medicine.

Long-term medical condition of persistently elevated blood pressure in the [[Artery|arteries]]. Usually symptomless, it is a major risk factor for [[Stroke|stroke]], coronary artery disease, [[Heart failure|heart failure]], atrial fibrillation and [[Dementia|dementia]], and a major cause of premature death worldwide. About 90–95% of cases are primary (essential), linked to lifestyle and genetic factors such as excess [[Salt|salt]], excess body weight, smoking and physical inactivity. High blood pressure is present when resting pressure is persistently at or above 130/80 mmHg (stage 1) or 140/90 mmHg (stage 2). Weight loss, exercise, less salt and a healthy diet can lower it, and up to three medications taken together can control it in 90% of people. About half of those affected do not know they have it.

Heart complications of high blood pressure, including [[Heart failure|heart failure]]. Its definition in International Classification of Diseases coding includes heart failure and other cardiac complications when death certificates state or imply that hypertension caused them. It caused 1.07 million deaths in 2013, up from 630,000 in 1990. Without heart failure it is usually symptomless; with it, symptoms include fatigue, shortness of breath, swollen ankles and irregular pulse. Because high blood pressure also drives [[Atherosclerosis|atherosclerosis]], death rates provide an incomplete measure of its burden.

Long, branching filamentous structure of a [[Fungus|fungus]], [[Oomycete|oomycete]] or actinobacterium. In most fungi, hyphae are the main mode of vegetative growth and collectively form a [[Mycelium|mycelium]]. Each hypha consists of one or more cells within a tubular [[Cell wall|cell wall]], usually made of [[Chitin|chitin]], unlike the cellulose walls of plants and oomycetes. Many hyphae are divided by cross-walls called septa, and some fungi are aseptate. Hyphae grow at their tips, driven by the *Spitzenkörper*, an aggregation of membrane-bound vesicles containing cell-wall components. Modified hyphae absorb nutrients in parasites and mycorrhizal fungi and make up much of the structure of [[Lichen|lichens]]. Hyphae have an average diameter of 4–6 μm.

Human condition involving [[Attention|focused attention]], reduced peripheral awareness and an enhanced capacity to respond to suggestion. Altered-state theories see it as a trance differing from ordinary consciousness, while non-state theories treat it as a type of [[Placebo|placebo]] effect, a redefined interaction with a therapist, or imaginative role enactment. A session usually begins with a hypnotic induction, a series of preliminary instructions and suggestions. Its therapeutic use is called hypnotherapy, and its use as entertainment is called stage hypnosis, a form of mentalism. Research indicates that hypnotizing an individual may aid the formation of false memories, and medical hypnosis is often considered [[Pseudoscience|pseudoscience]] or [[Quackery|quackery]].

[[Inorganic compound]] with the formula HClO, an acid that forms when [[Chlorine|chlorine]] dissolves in water. HClO and its hypochlorite anion are the primary disinfection agents of chlorine solutions, and it cannot be isolated from them. Its antimicrobial properties make the related [[Sodium hypochlorite|sodium hypochlorite]] an ingredient in many commercial [[Bleach|bleaches]], deodorants and disinfectants. Mammalian [[White blood cell|white blood cells]] generate it to help destroy bacteria and other microbes. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved products based on it for treating wounds. It was discovered in 1834 by the French chemist Antoine Jérôme Balard.
